newsitem.title: JAPAN: Opposition grows to Japan nuclear policy.
newsitem.headline: Opposition grows to Japan nuclear policy.

text.p: Japan's energy policy could be crippled because of mounting public opposition to nuclear power after a string of accidents, management errors and cover-up attempts, one of the country's top energy experts says.
The result could also lead to a build-up in plutonium stockpiles, said Kazuya Fujime, managing director of the Institute of Energy Economics (IEE).
"Unless plans to use plutonium at nuclear reactors move ahead, Japan could end up with surplus plutonium stockpiles," Fujime said in an interview.

That could cause an international outcry and raise fears about whether Japan was using the plutonium for non-peaceful purposes, said Fujime, whose institute is funded by several industries, including the oil and electricity sectors.
Resource-poor Japan has emphasised the recycling of nuclear fuel, which is reprocessed mostly overseas into plutonium and uranium, as a means of securing a stable energy source.
About one-third of Japan's electricity needs is nuclear generated.
Fast-breeder reactors (FBR), which produce more plutonium than they consume, and reprocessing plants are the pillars of the recycling system.
However, after an accident at Japan's prototype FBR, called Monju, in December 1995, plans to use plutonium reprocessed from spent fuel at FBRs have been shelved indefinitely.

Tokaimura, Japan's only nuclear fuel reprocessing plant, about 160 km (100 miles) northeast of Tokyo, has been shut since the country's worst-ever nuclear accident in March, in which 37 workers were exposed to mild radiation during a fire and explosion.
To reduce the growing stockpile of plutonium, the government in January issued a report urging utilities to use plutonium, in a form called MOX (mixed oxide), in their commercial reactors.

However, this system, in use in countries such as Germany and France, faces loud opposition from a Japanese public increasingly distrustful of the nuclear industry after a string of accidents, revelations of safety flaws and cover-up attempts, Fujime said.
Tokyo Electric Power Co and Kansai Electric Power Co have announced their intention to use MOX fuel, which is a blend of plutonium and uranium, at two reactors each from 1999 and 2000, respectively.

But the two cannot proceed without the approval of local authorities, and the governors of Niigata, Fukushima and Fukui prefectures, which have the largest concentration of nuclear power plants in Japan, have told Tokyo they cannot accept MOX fuel until the cause of the Monju accident is made clear.

Fujime said the increased anti-nuclear sentiment after last month's accident would make it hard to win that support. "It will be difficult to win approval with public confidence in nuclear power collapsing," Fujime said.

Although the plant operator, the Power Reactor and Nuclear Fuel Development Corp said the leaked radiation never reached harmful levels, public anger grew with subsequent revelations of safety flaws, including outdated fire fighting equipment and delays in alerting authorities and nearby residents.
The company was already reeling from the accident and a similar cover-up at the prototype Monju reactor, which involved a leak of sodium coolant.
No one was injured at that time but an official in charge of investigating the cover-up committed suicide.
Since the accident at Tokaimura, two electricity utilities have announced they would either delay or scrap plans to build nuclear power reactors because of strong local opposition.
